bib.title: Team of Thoughts: Efficient Test-time Scaling of Agentic Systems through Orchestrated Tool Calling

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Team of Thoughts: Efficient Test-time Scaling of Agentic Systems through Orchestrated Tool Calling", Jeffrey T. H. Wong, Zixi Zhang, Junyi Liu, Yiren Zhao (Imperial College London; Junyi Liu at Microsoft Research). arXiv 2602.16485v2, cs.CL, 25 Mar 2026. Preprint, no venue stated.

COVERAGE: All 13 pages, 48,987 chars, including the appendices (A-D). I read the whole text, skimming the references. Code link in the paper: github.com/JeffreyWong20/Team-of-Thoughts. No extraction faults and no embedded instructions.

CORE CLAIM: Treat different post-trained models (heterogeneous, not one model with personas) as tools. A central orchestrator picks which two to call using profiles the tool agents wrote about themselves, then aggregates their answers. The paper says this beats single models and a homogeneous role-play MAS (AgentVerse) on math and code.

HEADLINE NUMBERS (Table 1)
- Setup: 7 models (Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5-mini, Gemini 3 Flash, DeepSeek v3.2 Exp, GPT-OSS-20B, Qwen3-VL-235B, Phi-4). 2 tool agents are activated per call. The orchestrator is DeepSeek v3.2 for math and GPT-5 Mini for code. Calibration is a 10% random sample, or a 50/50 cross-calibration between AIME24 and AIME25. The paper does not state the number of runs or seeds.
- Team of Thoughts pass@1: AIME24 96.00, AIME25 95.33, HumanEval+ 95.33, MBPP+ 85.93, LiveCodeBench v6 77.91.
- AgentVerse (GPT-5-mini backbone) pass@1: AIME24 80.00, AIME25 60.00, HumanEval+ 91.46, MBPP+ 79.37, LCB 65.93.
- The best single model per benchmark is close: DeepSeek 94.67 on AIME24, 94.00 on AIME25, Claude 95.61 on HumanEval+, Gemini 84.44 on MBPP+, and DeepSeek 76.48 on LCB. The gain over the best single model is therefore 0.5 to 1.5 points at pass@1.
- It trails on some metrics. It loses to Claude at HumanEval+ pass@1 (95.33 vs 95.61). On LCB it loses to DeepSeek at pass@3 and pass@5 (85.05 vs 86.65, 87.91 vs 88.46).
- Majority voting (AIME only) scores 93.33 on both years.
- Figure 1 plots MBPP+ pass@5 against cost per sample. The cost is only in that figure, with no table of dollar figures.

ABLATIONS (all small benchmarks, mostly AIME24 and MBPP+)
- Tool-response content (Table 4): returning the final answer only beats returning the full reasoning trace. AIME25 pass@1 is 95.33 without traces vs 78.67 with them. MBPP+ pass@1 is 85.93 vs 80.90.
- Number of activated agents (Table 5, MBPP+, pool of 25): pass@1 is 82.75 at k=2 and 82.96 at k=4. It falls to 60.32 at k=8 and 60.63 at k=16. Pass@5 barely moves.
- Pool size (Table 6): k=2 stays stable from 10 to 100 models. At k=8, pass@1 drops from 74.97 at 10 models to 54.76 at 50 models. Selection agreement falls to 61.64% at 50 models.
- Orchestrator context (Table 8): going from 16K to 128K gives no gain. The authors conclude the bottleneck is aggregation, not context size.
- Orchestrator choice (Table 2) is task-dependent and not tied to model size. Qwen3-VL scores 26.67 on AIME24 as an orchestrator and Claude scores 66.67.
- Selection policy (Table 3, pass@1): self-assessment 96.00 on AIME24 and 85.93 on MBPP+. Orchestrator-led assessment is 92.67 and 85.77. Random is 94.00 and 84.44. Single model is 94.67 and 82.38. Orchestrator-led is below the single-model baseline on AIME24.
- Calibration set (Table 7, LCB): a categorized sample gives pass@1 81.65 vs 77.91 for random. Pass@5 is lower, 86.81 vs 87.91, because tool selection becomes less diverse.

QUOTES
- p.7: "incorporating full reasoning trajectories consistently degrades orchestration performance across all benchmarks."
- p.7: "increasing k yields negligible gains and eventually leads to performance degradation."
- p.8: "MAS performance is constrained by an orchestration bottleneck."
- p.9 (Limitations): "The orchestrator often fails to navigate expansive tool selection spaces, leading to suboptimal tool-calling sequences."

LIMITS
- The authors concede the central orchestrator is a bottleneck. Selection degrades as the pool grows, and variance rises under high context load.
- Only math and code benchmarks with exact-match or test-based scoring, all single-turn. The conclusion mentions multi-round, complex multi-agent tasks as future work.
- The paper gives no run counts, variance or confidence intervals. The margins over the best single model are small, and the AIME sets are only 30 problems each.
- The calibration dataset is tiny (18 questions for LCB). Calibration and test data come from the same benchmark, and AIME24 and AIME25 are used to calibrate each other. There is no held-out domain.
- No dollar-cost table. The efficiency claim rests on Figure 1 and on "massive parallelism" and token efficiency, which are asserted but not measured as latency or token counts.
- The AgentVerse baseline gets up to 1,000 retries on code tasks. It is a single baseline built on a single backbone.
- The Gaussian-mixture framing is labelled "a conceptual framework rather than a literal mechanical description".
- Most of the models are dated by now (2025 vintage).
- The paper says nothing about handoffs, subagent failure modes (beyond selection overload), role separation, or context isolation as such.

BUILDS ON: Test-time scaling (Snell et al. 2024; Wu et al. 2025; Brown et al. 2024, "Large language monkeys"). Reasoning topologies CoT (Wei et al. 2023), ToT (Yao et al. 2023), GoT (Besta et al., AAAI 2024). MAS frameworks AgentVerse (Chen et al., ICLR 2024), ChatDev (Qian et al., ACL 2024), MetaGPT (Hong et al. 2024), AutoGen (Wu et al. 2023), AgentNet (Yang et al. 2025b), Chain of Agents (Zhang et al., NeurIPS 2024) and "Society of Thoughts" (Kim et al. 2026). It also cites Anthropic's Claude Code agent teams docs (2026).

FIT TO NOTE 07-orchestration.md: Partial. It supports three narrow points. (1) The join step: pass back final answers only, not traces (the context-firewall point, Table 4). (2) A fan-out of 2 to 4 beats 8 to 16, with pass@1 collapsing at 8 (Table 5). (3) A single orchestrator's selection and aggregation are the bottleneck when the pool is large (Table 6). It is weak on role separation, handoffs, topologies and when not to go multi-agent, and it is test-time-scaling research on benchmarks, not a harness paper. It does not fit another note in 03-harness-engineering/notes better as far as I can tell. I did not read the notes. Use it as a "sharpens" citation for the join step, with a caveat on setup: coding and math benchmarks only, no run counts reported.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 1 (p.1), MBPP+ pass@5 accuracy against cost per sample, with the single-model Pareto front. It shows the cost and accuracy claim in one image, but cost is only readable from the plot.

PROBLEMS: None with extraction. Table 1 cells are slightly jumbled in the text layer (bold values run together), but the numbers above were cross-checked against the row text.
